title: How to Make a Professional Presentation with AI in 10 Minutes

scenes.chapterTitle: Intro: 10 free AI decks, then pay?
scenes.badge: Gamma's free plan: 400 credits, about 40 per AI deck
scenes.sub: Then the credits never refresh (June 2026 pricing breakdown)
scenes.text: Gamma's free plan gives you four hundred credits, and creating a deck with AI costs about forty. That's roughly ten presentations, and then those credits never refresh. Meanwhile, PowerPoint now builds decks with Copilot, and Google Slides started building full presentations from a single prompt this summer. So which one should you use, and can you really make a professional presentation in ten minutes? In this video, I'll walk you through a ten minute workflow, what each tool needs, what it costs, and the mistakes that make AI decks look cheap.

scenes.title: A real deck in 10 minutes
scenes.sub: PowerPoint, Google Slides or Gamma: what works
scenes.text: First, what does professional mean here? It doesn't mean fancy animations. It means a clear message, one idea per slide, readable text, and numbers you can defend. AI is very good at the first draft: the outline, the layout, the wording. It's not good at knowing your audience or checking your facts. So the plan is simple. You spend two minutes thinking, let the AI do the heavy lifting, and spend the rest of the time fixing what it gets wrong. Everything here was checked against Microsoft, Google and Gamma pages in November twenty twenty six.

items.text: What should they decide or do?

footer.text: A vague prompt gives a generic deck

scenes.text: Step one, minutes zero to two: write a four line brief before you open any tool. Line one: who is the audience? Your boss, a client, a class? Line two: what should they decide or do after the talk? Line three: how many slides and how long you'll speak. Ten slides for a ten minute talk is a good start. Line four: the one thing they must remember. Paste this brief into whichever tool you use. A vague prompt gives you a generic deck. A clear brief gives you a draft that already sounds like your talk.

scenes.chapterTitle: Copilot in PowerPoint: how it works

items.text: Pick a Brand Kit, if you have one
Or start from a Word document

footer.text: Tip: Word file under 24 MB, using Word Styles

scenes.text: Option one: Copilot in PowerPoint. According to Microsoft's support page, updated in October, you start a new presentation and open Copilot from the icon at the bottom right. If your company set one up, you can pick a Brand Kit, with your logos, fonts and colors. Then you paste your brief. Copilot may ask follow up questions about the audience, length and imagery, and then builds the deck. You can also start from a Word document. Microsoft's tip: it works best with Word files smaller than twenty four megabytes that use proper headings, known as Word Styles.

items.name: One file
items.desc: One Word file at a time on home plans

items.name: PDF too
items.desc: Work accounts can also use a PDF

items.name: Word limit
items.desc: A cap on words per prompt

footer.text: Source: Microsoft FAQ, Copilot in PowerPoint

scenes.text: A few limits from Microsoft's own FAQ. First, the license. If you don't see Copilot, it may simply not be included in your Microsoft three sixty five plan. On home plans, you can point it at one Word file at a time. Work accounts can also use a PDF. Microsoft also says Copilot is limited in the number of words it can process per prompt, but it doesn't publish the number, so very long documents may get cut short. And while many languages work, quality is expected to be highest in English. Check what your plan includes before you count on it.

Option two: Gemini in Google Slides. Google announced at the end of June twenty twenty six that one prompt in the side panel can now build a full multi slide deck. It can pull in your Drive files, even match the style of a deck you attach. And here's the part I like: it shows you the outline first, so you can edit it before any slides are built. The result is normal, editable slides. Google lists it for Business and Enterprise Standard and Plus, and for personal Google AI Pro and Ultra plans. At launch, it supports English in the United States only.

footer.text: Free first. Pay only if you use it weekly.

scenes.text: Option three: Gamma, a standalone AI presentation app. It works from a prompt, pasted notes or a document. Prices change often, so here's a pricing breakdown published in June twenty twenty six. Free is zero dollars, with four hundred starter credits that never refresh. Plus is nine dollars per seat per month. Pro is eighteen, and Ultra is ninety. So Plus works out to about one hundred eight dollars a year. My suggestion is simple: start on the free plan, and pay only if you find yourself making decks weekly. Check Gamma's own pricing page before you buy.

scenes.chapterTitle: Gamma free plan: the fine print
scenes.text: Now the fine print on Gamma's free plan, from the same June breakdown. Creating a deck with AI costs forty credits, and each extra card costs five more. You get up to ten cards per prompt, and in Gamma a card is basically a slide. You can export to PDF, PowerPoint or Google Slides, which is great, because you can finish the deck in the app you already use. But the made with Gamma badge stays on everything you share or export, and free users can't buy extra credits. Once the four hundred are gone, you upgrade or stop.

Here's the full ten minute workflow. Minutes zero to two: write the brief. Minutes two to three: generate, and fix the outline before the slides are built, if your tool shows it. Minutes three to six: go slide by slide. Cut the text to a few short lines, check every number, and replace anything vague with your real example. Minutes six to eight: one design pass. Use your company template, keep fonts consistent, and swap generic pictures for real charts or screenshots. Minutes eight to ten: click through the deck out loud once. The AI drafts. You decide.

scenes.chapterTitle: 5 mistakes that make AI decks look cheap

items.name: Unchecked facts
items.desc: AI doesn't verify numbers or claims

items.name: Wall of text
items.desc: Cut every slide to a few lines

items.name: Image-only slides
items.desc: Text baked into a picture can't be edited

items.name: Generic stock art
items.desc: Use your own charts and screenshots

items.name: Private data
items.desc: Only add files you'd show on a slide

footer.text: Your name is on the deck, not the AI's

scenes.text: Now, five mistakes that make AI decks look cheap. One: unchecked facts. These tools don't verify claims, so every number needs a source you trust. Two: a wall of text. AI loves full sentences. Cut every slide down to a few lines. Three: image only slides. Some features turn a slide into a picture, and text inside a picture can't be edited later. Four: generic stock art that has nothing to do with your point. Five: private data. Only add files you'd be comfortable showing on a slide. Remember, your name is on the deck, not the AI's.

footer.text: Or ask any free AI chat for the outline, then build it yourself

scenes.text: So which one should you use? If you already work in PowerPoint and your Microsoft plan includes Copilot, start there, especially if your company has a Brand Kit. If you live in Google Workspace on an eligible plan, Gemini in Slides is the smoothest, because you review the outline first. If neither plan covers it, try Gamma's free plan for your next few decks and export to PowerPoint or Slides. And with no budget at all, ask any free AI chat assistant to turn your brief into a slide by slide outline, then build it yourself. That still saves most of the time.

scenes.title: AI drafts, you decide
scenes.next: AI Meeting Notes: Never Write Minutes Again
scenes.text: So yes, a professional presentation in ten minutes is realistic now, as long as you treat AI as the drafter and yourself as the editor. Write a clear brief, review the outline, fix the facts, and do one design pass. Now I want to hear from you. What's the next presentation you have to make? Tell me in the comments. If this helped, subscribe to Future Money Lab, and I'll see you in the next video.
